articles.title: Childhood dementia should be more widely recognised, mother says
articles.summary: An affected mother says she cannot think of a worse diagnosis for a child than childhood dementia.
articles.body:
The mother of a two-year-old girl diagnosed with a form of childhood dementia has said she wants greater recognition of the term after their shock at what they felt was a lack of awareness.

Emily's daughter, Leni, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome last year - a rare, genetic disorder which leads to severe cognitive decline and a loss of motor skills.

Emily, from Sevenoaks in Kent, said: "It is catastrophic, I can't think of a worse diagnosis for your child, or for anyone, and yet no-one knows about it."

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) said it was "working hard to find new ways to slow down the progress of dementia, speed up diagnosis and improve our understanding of the disease".

Sanfilippo Syndrome is one of more than 140 conditions that can cause childhood dementia - a term that brings individually quite rare conditions under one umbrella.

Emily said: "Grouping them together gives us a much more powerful voice and the ability to make significant change.

"The goal is to make real change. It's not to get one child access to treatment, it's to get real change made at government level that then benefits nationwide."

Sanfilippo Syndrome progressively damages the brain, causing children to lose skills they have already learnt, including speech and mobility.

The condition is caused when people are low in, or missing, certain enzymes in the body. Many children affected do not reach adulthood.

According to the MPS Society, which supports those with diseases like Sanfilippo, "there is currently treatment for symptoms as they arise, but no cure for the underlying disease".

Emily said: "At the moment, Leni is like any other two-year-old. She is doing really well which is obviously amazing, but it also makes it really, really painful because we have so much to lose."

Emily said regression usually starts at about three years-old.

The family has released a book called Saving Leni which tells their daughter's story.

Sophie Thomas, Interim chief executive of The MPS Society said: "Ultimately, recognition would help professionals understand the condition, it would improve access to support, encourage investment in research and make sure childhood dementia is considered in policy and service planning."

A DHSC spokesperson said: "Neurodegenerative conditions such as Sanfilippo syndrome have a devastating impact and our thoughts are with Leni and her family.

"We are making sure patients with rare diseases get a definite diagnosis faster, while improving access to specialist care, treatment and drugs.

"At the same time we are working hard to find new ways to slow down the progress of dementia, speed up diagnosis and improve our understanding of the disease."

Meanwhile, for Leni, there is a possibility of taking part in a clinical trial later this year.

Emily said: "For the first time since Leni's diagnosis we actually have some hope for the future.

"We have received such a huge amount of support and generosity from people and there is now real hope of Leni accessing a clinical trial that could change her life."

articles.title: IndiGo engineer stays with mother inside Noida bus, both die
articles.summary: IndiGo engineer Shashank Gupta and mother Sunita identified among nine killed in Noida Yamuna Expressway bus fire; short circuit in AC wiring suspected.
articles.body: NOIDA: The last thing 28-year-old Shashank Gupta told the bus driver was that he would step off the burning vehicle only after his mother did. He never got the chance.Late on Wednesday night, a private AC sleeper bus (BR32PA8647) bound from Kashmere Gate in Delhi to Mahoba caught fire near the 33km milestone of Yamuna Expressway in Jewar.By the time the flames were doused, nine of the 35 people aboard were dead. 26 passengers, both drivers and the conductor, made it out alive. Shashank and his mother Sunita Gupta (47) did not.Their badly burnt bodies were identified on Friday, not by their faces, but by what survived of them. Family members recognised Sunita by her height and Shashank by a ring he wore.The two had boarded the bus, operated by Raj Kalpana Travels, almost by accident. Sunita had been living with her son in Gurgaon for about a month, receiving treatment for knee pain that had left her struggling to walk.When her husband Neeraj’s brother suffered a heart attack in Charkhari, Mahoba, three days before the fire, mother and son decided to travel there together. Train tickets were unavailable, so they took seats towards the rear of the sleeper bus instead.According to Neeraj, passengers on board had complained of a burning smell in the cabin well before flames were visible. He alleged the complaints went unheeded and the bus was not stopped, a delay he believes cost lives that might otherwise have been saved.Some passengers earlier told TOI that they had raised an alarm with the driver and conductor, who allegedly continued smoking inside the cabin rather than pulling over. Soon after, flames started near the driver’s seat, and smoke filled the bus within minutes.What followed was chaos. As flames spread, some passengers smashed windows and leapt from the moving bus while others rushed to the front and got off once the driver pulled over.“Amid that scramble, Sunita, unable to move quickly because of her injured knee, fell behind. Other passengers told me that Shashank refused to leave her side,” Neeraj said.“The driver and conductor both urged my son to get out while he still could. He refused, telling them he would only leave with his mother. He stayed, trying to pull her towards the door as the cabin filled with smoke, until neither of them could breathe and lost consciousness,” Neeraj said.Shashank worked as an engineer with IndiGo Airlines in Gurgaon. He is survived by his father and a younger brother Nikhil (22), who is still in college. Their bodies were taken back to Charkhari on Friday.Police also released the body of Omprakash Dhan Singh, the ninth victim identified. Six others were named a day earlier: Shruti Rawat (28) of Chhatarpur, Madhya Pradesh, Saroj Gupta (52), Mayank Gupta (28) and Usha Devi (65), all of Hamirpur, Devendra Sahay Bhardwaj (60) of Hisar, Haryana, and Har Sharan Gupta (55) of Jalaun.All nine bodies have been returned to their families following autopsy, police said. articles.title: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to university
articles.summary: This new stage of parenthood is emotional - but learning how to let go can help you cope.
articles.body:
Luke felt overwhelmed with both pride and grief after dropping his son off at university for the first time.

"It feels like a brutal adjustment," he says.

"After 18 years of seeing him every day and taking care of him, I miss him so much and I don't really know what to do with myself."

Like other parents we have spoken to, Luke (not his real name) and his wife have felt compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers with children living in the same halls of residence, as well as a university-wide version with more than 2,000 members.

At first, being in these groups felt helpful for practical information, particularly in the weeks before his son headed to university, Luke says. But now they're feeding his anxiety.

"People will post things like: 'Is it normal to spend so much time in your room?'; 'I'm worried my daughter is struggling to make friends'; 'My child isn't replying to messages - how often are people hearing from theirs?'"

There have also been questions about Amazon parcel logistics, requests to borrow cereal bowls and what tog duvet other people's children were given.

Luke thinks these kinds of social media groups have fuelled his temptation to keep checking his son's location on a tracking app "to make sure he is going out enough and finding friends".

Because his messages and calls go largely unanswered, Luke will also watch videos posted on the university's social media accounts, hoping to catch a glimpse of his son among the throngs of Freshers. Other parents have sheepishly confessed they're doing the same.

Across universities, some enterprising parents have set up the sort of WhatsApp group chats you'd more typically find being used when children are at school. Only rather than asking after lost jumpers and what day PE is, these groups might be used to try to parent long-distance.

"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.

She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help.

"These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.

Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.

Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves.

"Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'"

"Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."

'Students should be figuring it out for themselves'

A big part of going to university is about being independent, says Manchester University student Archie Forde, 19, who has heard stories of parents "pinging phones at 3am and calling their kids 12 times a week".

He thinks parents turning to social media groups have "mostly fair concerns" but are going about things in the wrong way.

The groups can be "echo chambers where everyone just spins each other out about their kids", he says, and suggests having a proper conversation with your child about boundaries, before university starts.

Every family will have different ideas about what is overbearing, but a student shouldn't have the worry of choosing between "cutting back parents' communication and ruining that relationship, or responding to a flurry of texts at pre-drinks and detaching yourself from the social situation".

Writing a letter or sending a parcel - without the expectation of a getting a response - could be a good way to let your child know you're thinking of them, "without it feeling like a demand", says child psychologist Laverne Antrobus.

Perhaps negotiate a time to check in with them, "and be prepared to not always have long conversations," she says.

And when you do speak to your child, "make sure your curiosity is genuine, rather than half-informed by the surveillance you've been doing".

"Already knowing where they've been and what they've been up to makes for an unrewarding conversation with them and children are bright - they will know."

Rayyah says she looks forward to properly catching up when she goes home.

"If you've spent months being closely monitored it might feel as if you haven't really been away or gained any independence; it could feel frustrating."

'I didn't know who I was without the kids'

Having seen three children off to university, Nichola McClellan wants to reassure parents that it does get easier. Based in Cheshire, she shares her experience of being an "empty nester" on social media.

"It's a huge emotional adjustment after years of your life revolving around your children, so we need to give ourselves time and permission to miss them.

"I think back to how lost I felt. I didn't know who I was without the kids.

"They're learning how to leave," she says, "but we're learning how to let go."

Rather than expect constant contact, Nichola sends "little no-pressure messages" on their family WhatsApp group.

"'Love you', 'proud of you' - things that don't require an answer."

They have a proper catch-up roughly once a week, and she has learned not to take it personally if she doesn't hear from them.

"Sometimes that is a really good sign, it means they're getting on with this new life you've spent all those years preparing them for.

"You don't stop being a parent when they leave home - but you do get the opportunity to rediscover parts of yourself that perhaps got a little lost along the way. There really is so much to look forward to."

Psychologist Charlotte Armitage shares her advice to help parents cope with this new stage of parenthood:

Think twice before you post on a parents' group Feeling anxious, bereft or excluded is normal, but those feelings don't always require action. Before posting on a group or stepping in, Armitage says ask yourself: "Is this a genuine safety issue? Have I given my young adult the chance to deal with it? Am I helping them become more capable, or managing my own anxiety?"

Steer clear of constant checking and tracking or intervening These may soothe you in the short term, but can inadvertently communicate to your young adult: "I am not sure you can cope without me." Of course, parents should step in when there is a safeguarding concern or risk to their child's wellbeing

The most valuable message you can send To help your child settle into adult life, Armitage says the most valuable message you can send is: "I am here if you need me and I believe you can do this."

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV warns AI could undermine humanity during France visit
articles.summary: Thousands gather in Paris as the pope warns against a ‘paradise of machines’ at the Elysee Palace.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has warned that artificial intelligence, which he referred to as a “paradise of machines”, and other emerging technologies could undermine humanity by posing fundamental questions about what it means to be human.

Thousands gathered to welcome the pope in France on Friday, shortly after he raised existential questions about technological advancement and human rights during his opening speech to President Emmanuel Macron and authorities at the Elysee Palace and then to diplomats and United Nations employees at the headquarters of UNESCO, the UN culture and education organisation.

“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment,” Pope Leo said beside Macron.

Scientific progress should not turn “into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death”, the pope said, a few months after France passed a landmark bill legalising assisted dying.

He reaffirmed the Vatican’s opposition to nuclear weapons, stating that the nuclear deterrence doctrine was “mistaken” as it was heightening a new arms race.

The pope identified AI as one of the greatest challenges currently facing humanity since the very beginning of his pontificate, dedicating his first encyclical to the topic to call for significant regulation and for developers to work for the common good.

“The paradox has become increasingly evident: while ‘intelligence’ is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons, whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, are rejected and discarded,” he said.

The pope had earlier told reporters that he was pleased that his message was being heard by AI developers and hoped the dialogue would continue between tech companies and the Vatican.

“And I think from their perspective, many of them, they’re very much open to looking for ways of making sure that AI does not displace or ultimately destroy humanity, but rather is a tool for human beings,” he said.

The pope’s four-day trip marks the first official papal visit to France in 18 years. While secularism is enshrined in the country’s constitution, the pontiff stressed that “authentic secularity” should not exclude religion “from the public sphere or from education”.

Thousands of worshippers cheered Leo on Friday as he stepped up to pray and called those gathered at a stadium near Paris the “saints of France”. Earlier in the afternoon, the pope crossed central Paris in his popemobile.

The Vatican estimated that about 300,000 people had come out to see the pontiff on Friday.

articles.title: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue
articles.summary: Bare nails - or nails that appear that way - are a growing trend. But is it as innocent as it seems?
articles.body:
In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all.

"It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.

These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."

Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.

In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".

But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.

Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say.

"That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC.

"They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."

For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.

Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.

For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.

Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail.

"It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."

Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth.

"I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'

"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."

Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.

Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.

But beauty magazines have declared " All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures ", that " Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol " of "Polished Women" and that " Manicures Are No Longer Classy ".

And now, there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it.

At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya.

Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year.

"It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home."

Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says.

"I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money."

But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister.

Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro.

"Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.

Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.

A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.

And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.

But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.

Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Dianna Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.

"These were times that it was hard for black women to be able to express themselves," says celebrity nail artist Celeste Hampton.

"[Nail art] allowed black women to express our form of softness, our form of femininity, our form of beauty."

And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.

But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says.

"The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now.

"The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."

Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine.

"The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."

Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women.

"I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."

Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised.

"We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says.

"Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"

"For me, it's like just stop judging ourselves and everybody else... Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't," she says.

"I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?

"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

articles.title: Silent Hill Townfall: Iconic horror game gets a clever Scottish makeover
articles.summary: One of gaming's biggest horror franchises has come to the UK. Can it live up to the original?
articles.body:
As I creep through the heavy fog of Silent Hill: Townfall, I'm met by an oddly familiar sight amid the terror - a sign for a Sunday roast.

For the first time, one of gaming's biggest horror franchises - created in Japan but traditionally set in the US - has come to the UK, set on a fictional Scottish island.

Jon McKellan, director at Glaswegian developers Screen Burn, told me taking on the mega brand was an "absolutely terrifying" prospect for the relatively small team.

As a fan of the games, I was keen to find out what one of the most iconic survival horror series looks like in Scotland - and whether it can live up to its legacy.

I played Silent Hill: Townfall, which was released on Thursday, on my PlayStation 5, and it ran well, though there have been some reports from others of performance issues.

Set in 1996, the game follows the plight of an American man called Simon Ordell, who washes up on St Amelia with a red hospital ID band around his wrist and an IV drip in his arm.

As is to be expected from the Silent Hill games, the real reasons why you're there and what's going on are teased as you progress through the story in a typically vague fashion.

The team took inspiration for the setting from the tiny fishing village of St Monans in Fife.

For those concerned the game might lean into any typical Scottish stereotypes, McKellan told me he wanted it to feel "authentic and natural".

"It's not tartan everywhere, but if you grew up in a working-class town in the 90s, you will get a lot of the references," he said.

In Townfall I walked past film-quality models of red pillar boxes, 20 mph speed limit signs and charity collection boxes shaped like guide dogs.

Not since 2006, when I had to storm Manchester Cathedral in Resistance: Fall of Man, have I felt an oddly patriotic attachment to game areas or objects.

To save the game, I had to use a phone, which often meant stepping inside a "coins and card" telephone box - a sight instantly familiar to anyone old enough to remember them on British streets.

Meanwhile, a level set in a council estate leans into the concrete starkness of the area's looming grey buildings.

While some may question why the main character is American rather than Scottish given the setting, there are narrative reasons why Simon is more of an outsider to this community, which are slowly drip-fed into cutscenes and in-game documents.

For the most part I was intrigued by the story, which, like many of the previous games, explores themes of trauma and guilt sensitively. This edition also touches on ideas around the impact of big corporations on small communities, which brought added relevance to the setting of an isolated seaside town.

I soon had to face the island's monsters - gnarled, fleshy beings with axe-like heads or mangled faces.

While St Amelia's inhabitants might not quite live up to the heights of Silent Hill 2's mannequins for sudden frights, their speed and general nastiness were still enough to make me want to run away as fast as possible.

Even when I picked up weapons such as a plank of wood or a steel pipe, a series staple, there was never much sense that I had the upper hand.

These all degrade over time, and though I did eventually get a gun, bullets are scarce, meaning I still had to sneak around rather than face threats head-on.

"We don't do jump scares, really," said McKellan - although I can think of a few alarming times playing the game I vehemently disagreed with that statement.

The fear is dialled up an extra notch by Byron Bullock's rich sound design, with the music swelling almost unbearably intensely when spluttering nasties stumbled closer.

Composer Pilotpriest, also known as Anthony Scott Burns, deserves recognition too for his hauntingly bleak soundtrack.

I think it says a lot that I closed every door I opened behind me in the game, in the naive hope it might stop monsters following - even at moments when there were none around.

Simon soon picks up a handheld CRT device to help with sneaking - a clever updated version of another staple of the Silent Hill series: the crackling radio.

This piece of retro tech - basically a small portable TV - gives you a fuzzy image of nearby monsters on its screen, so you have some idea of where they are in order to avoid them, though it can get a little fiddly if there are several nearby.

"I think it lends itself well to horror when the technology is a bit frail, a bit outdated," said McKellan.

"You don't feel safe when those kinds of things are fragile."

Later sections where you rely on even cruder tech to spot enemies ratchet up the tension further, at the expense of making the gameplay much slower.

Thankfully, there are often other cues as to the whereabouts of your fleshy foes, such as flickering lights and their awful, gurgling cries.

Reviews of the game have championed its atmosphere, with IGN's Tristan Ogilvie calling it "oppressively ominous".

Silent Hill: Townfall has three difficulty settings for combat - easy, normal and nightmare (there are also two settings for puzzles, with one giving more hints).

I played on normal, though there were one or two sections with a new, super-strong and fast single enemy where I considered changing to easy.

These were the most aggravating parts of the game for me, despite having played and loved Alien: Isolation, a game McKellan also worked on, which has a lot of challenging bits where you have to avoid the powerful Alien.

Chris Scullion, deputy editor at Video Games Chronicle said these moments were "deeply frustrating" and caused the game, which he otherwise found "outstanding", to come "grinding to a halt".

Townfall is not the first time the series has strayed away from the original game's location in America, 2025's Silent Hill f was set in 1960s rural Japan.

This sparked a conversation about whether a game can be part of the series yet not be set in or around the fictional eponymous town.

The series' lead producer at Konami Motoi Okamoto told me the team were looking at various areas to potentially set the next games, from "other parts of Europe" to "Latin America".

Games journalist and self-proclaimed "Silent Hillian" Vikki Blake told me the latest game exceeded her expectations, though she's still not convinced these newer games truly fit under the Silent Hill name.

After my playthrough, I can see why Konami are pushing ahead with the idea to let other studios breathe new life into the franchise and take it to different destinations.

Townfall is a brutal, grim journey - uneven in parts, but clever - and full of immense tension and inventive game design, the kind that is needed to push a nearly 30-year-old franchise forward.

Okamoto has also expressed his desire to release a Silent Hill game every year - whether that be a remaster, remake, or entirely new material.

If more new studios can keep the games feeling as fresh as this, we may eventually become like one of the series' many troubled protagonists – forgetting why we ever needed the titular town at all.

articles.title: 'Indie and punk music made me feel I was betraying my race'
articles.summary: Big Joanie's Stephanie Phillips sets out the history of black people and alternative music.
articles.body:
Growing up in Wolverhampton, Stephanie Phillips says she was initially pretty much into the same chart music as her friends.

But alongside TLC, Aaliyah and Destiny's Child, she developed a passion for rock, indie and punk.

"It was music that meant a lot to me as someone who was very shy and needed an outlet," she said. Yet she felt compelled to keep that passion hidden.

"There was always this idea that black people weren't really into alternative music, or punk," the musician, journalist and author told the BBC.

"When I first got into alternative music I felt like I was betraying my race, and had to keep my love of rock practically secret," she writes in her new book.

"There was a particular way that I was supposed to move through the world and being super into this genre was seen as something that wasn't for black people."

In We Were Here, the Big Joanie singer and guitarist charts the role of black artists in creating, shaping and transforming rock 'n' roll, punk and alternative music.

Phillips argues black artists never disappeared from the scene but were often forgotten, overlooked or deliberately excluded.

"There was this insinuation that we weren't really part of those histories," she said, "but when you look back, there was so much there."

She says the phrase "black weirdo" captures both how she felt and how others viewed her involvement in the punk scene.

The lead singer of ska and 2 Tone group The Selecter, Pauline Black, agrees.

The pair are set to take part in an event together as part of Black History Month, in Coventry.

"Although what I do still comes from the genre of black music, I was one of those weirdos in a way because I come from a folk background, and you can't get much whiter than that," said Black.

"Certainly when I was growing up if you weren't into Tamla, you weren't into soul - which I am, but didn't particularly want to do music like that - then nobody really understands.

"If you want to be a punk, and are black and a woman it's very difficult."

The book explores figures including Sister Rosetta Tharpe and Jimi Hendrix before moving through later genres, from heavy rock to pioneering punk acts such as Bad Brains and Pure Hell.

"We've always known that black people were essential to the creation of rock and roll," Phillips said.

"They're also essential to the creation and continuation of so many different genres that came off of that."

Tharpe, whose guitar work helped shape artists including Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley and Little Richard, was "pivotal" to the emergence of rock'n'roll, Phillips said.

Yet she was largely forgotten after her death in 1973 before being rediscovered decades later.

Phillips argues these histories were often overlooked as music journalism grew more influential.

Publications such as Rolling Stone helped define the archetypal rock star, she argues, often favouring white male artists while overlooking many groundbreaking black performers.

Segregation also shaped the music industry and charts until the mid-1960s.

"The threat of the colour line being breached was terrifying in America," she said. "It wasn't just in schools or public spaces, it was in culture too."

Pioneering black punk bands such as Bad Brains were frequently under-recognised despite their influence, Phillips said.

"They completely changed what hardcore could be. They had the technical proficiency to play harder, to play faster," she added.

"People think black people haven't been there. It's like, well, we probably have been, the question is whether it was documented properly."

After moving to London, Phillips became involved in the independent DIY punk scene, which she said was welcoming to women, non-binary and trans people.

But despite the city's diversity, there were still only a handful of black people involved.

"It still made me feel a bit of an outsider," she said.

In response she co-founded Big Joanie, describing the group as a black feminist punk band.

"It was exciting creating a space where black women could exist outside all those expectations," she said.

The book also examines how black artists within alternative music have faced hostile or distorted media coverage.

She points to Skunk Anansie's Skin, who was often portrayed through the lens of her appearance rather than her music.

"The only way they would speak about her is either that they found her scary or they couldn't take their eyes off her," she explained.

"They were seen as outsiders and their music wasn't really as well championed as other artists."

Bloc Party frontman Kele Okereke experienced similar treatment, including being outed by a music magazine.

Interviewing him for the book, Phillips said it was clear the experience had remained painful.

"The shyness and vulnerability of one of the few black men in the indie world was often being interpreted as hostility," she said.

Black recalled that a famous 1980 photograph of her alongside Debbie Harry, Poly Styrene of X-Ray Spex and other leading female artists, featured on the cover of New Music News magazine, was billed as representing "the women in rock".

"And I suppose they needed a couple of black women in there as well," she said.

"But it was interesting they couldn't put one woman on the cover.

"In those days their ethos was that if you put a black face on the cover, particularly if it's not a male black face, then you're not really going to sell many copies."

Even today, Phillips argues black artists were often forgotten, overlooked or deliberately excluded.

She cites Nova Twins, who took out a bank loan to record their debut album which received rave reviews but they still struggled to find a label, she said.

The issue is personal, she added, recalling the challenges of securing support for Big Joanie's early releases.

"You do have to work harder. It can be exhausting."

Now based in Birmingham, the author is taking part in a series of events discussing the issues raised in the book, including a conversation with The Selecter's lead singer at Warwick Arts Centre.

"I'm really interested to hear what makes Stephanie tick," said Black.

"She would have grown up a generation behind me, so her experience would have been different, but I don't think the industry had changed significantly by the time she formed Big Joanie.

"I think she's done an extraordinary job, both with her band and with the book.

"So it's 'up the weirdos', is what I say."

We Were Here: A History of Black People and Alternative Music by Stephanie Phillips is published by Faber .

She is in conversation with Pauline Black at Warwick Arts Centre on 15 October and appearing at Supersonic Festival in Birmingham on 18 November.

articles.title: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war?
articles.summary: Exploring the issues behind the escalation of tensions between the TPLF and the national army.
articles.body:
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.

Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.

There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.

This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.

It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.

The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.

This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.

This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.

The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.

For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.

It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.

At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.

When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.

Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.

The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.

An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.

There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.

The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.

Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.

When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.

The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.

For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.

The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.

But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.

This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.

A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.

Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.

Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.

So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.

TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.

Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.

As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.

It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.

During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.

Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.

Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.

What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?

Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.

The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.

Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.

This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.

The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.

What is being done to stop the fighting?

The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.

It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.

The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.

The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.

The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.

Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.

The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.

The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.

There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.

The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.

The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

articles.title: Iran says it awaits US response on seven-day roadmap to end war
articles.summary: Tehran says the plan would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks within a week if Washington agrees.
articles.body:
Iran has formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to end its war with the United States and is now awaiting Washington’s response, according to Tehran’s top diplomat.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed the plan to reporters outside the United Nations Security Council on Friday, saying it had been conveyed to Washington through Qatar.

“The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.

Araghchi noted that initial steps would take four to five days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day and “on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects”, referring to Iran’s nuclear programme.

Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.

In return, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed before the war, and which has become Tehran’s main point of leverage.

“The choice now rests with the United States,” Araghchi said.

“Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. I can tell you if there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.”

Ending all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Yemen and Lebanon, was reportedly among Tehran’s demands.

The proposal, which aims to end the war that has entered its seventh month, closely mirrors a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between Tehran and Washington on June 17, after Qatari and Pakistani mediation, which set a 60-day window for talks but collapsed within weeks.

Technical and vague terms over control of shipping through Hormuz led to disputes, as Iran began firing on vessels it accused of ignoring its authorisation rules, prompting US President Donald Trump to declare the deal “over” in July.

The US has since sporadically struck Iranian territory and coastal areas in response.

Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Witkoff said the meeting was “lengthy” and that he hoped the talks would “ prove constructive and promising .”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Fox News this week that ending the war was now up to Washington. “It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not,” he said.

A White House official told CNN the Trump administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”.

“Basically nothing has really changed,” said Cyrus Schayegh of the Geneva Graduate Institute, arguing Iran wants to keep the leverage it gained during the war, while Washington resists returning to the June framework.

It appears unlikely that the new deal will make major progress before the US midterm elections in November, though Araghchi said Friday it “would be better” to reach one beforehand.

Qatar, a key mediator in the conflict, said its foreign minister spoke with Pezeshkian on Friday about de-escalation and the conditions for renewed dialogue.

articles.title: US court rules against Kalshi, says states can regulate prediction markets
articles.summary: US appeals courts have varied on regulation of prediction markets, opening the door to US Supreme Court debate.
articles.body:
A United States appeals court has found that states can regulate prediction markets, ruling against a bid by the company Kalshi to exempt so-called event contracts from state gambling laws.

The Friday ruling by the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals in Cincinnati is the latest in an unfolding debate about oversight of prediction markets, whose explosive growth has prompted ethical and regulatory questions.

The decision also deepens a divide among federal appeals courts regarding the authority of state and federal regulators to regulate such markets, opening up the possibility that the US Supreme Court could weigh in on the matter.

Two other federal appeals courts have previously addressed questions of whether prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws. The 9th Circuit in San Francisco ruled last month that Kalshi’s event contracts are subject to Nevada’s gambling laws, while the 3rd Circuit in Philadelphia said in April that Kalshi’s contracts are not subject to New Jersey’s.

In Friday’s ruling, Judge Julia Smith Gibbons wrote for the unanimous three-judge panel that Ohio and Tennessee can regulate event contracts under their gambling laws.

Prediction markets have become increasingly popular in the US. They allow users to place bets on everything from sporting events and presidential elections to cultural developments and the prospects of a deal between the US and Iran on the latter’s nuclear programme.

Experts have raised concerns about the proliferation of prediction markets and betting apps, especially for young people.

The state of New York filed a lawsuit against the prediction market Polymarket on Thursday, arguing that it is operating as an unlicensed gambling operation. The company responded by stating that it would “fight for its users”.

“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement.

articles.title: ‘Choice now rests with US’: Iran offers America 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz and resume stalled talks on its nuclear programme, with
articles.body: Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz and resume stalled talks on its nuclear programme, with foreign minister Abbas Araghchi saying the next move now rests with Washington.Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the waterway if the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that includes Lebanon, according to Araghchi's remarks to reporters outside the United Nations Security Council on Friday."If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," he said.“The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” Araghchi said.Iran's proposal would also restart talks with Washington on a final agreement covering Tehran's nuclear programme.How Iran's seven-day plan would workAraghchi said the initial steps would take four to five days, with the Strait of Hormuz reopening on the sixth day.“And on day seven, the talks with the U.S. will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” he said.Araghchi said the measures Washington would need to take were already included in the memorandum of understanding agreed between Iran and the United States in June."The actions that the United States should should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU," he said.The proposal was conveyed to Washington through Qatar, which has played a key role in mediating between Iran and the United States.Hormuz becomes Iran's main bargaining toolIran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central source of leverage in its confrontation with Washington.Before the war, about a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas passed through the strategic waterway, according to the supplied report. Disruptions have affected energy markets beyond the Middle East and created political pressure on the Trump administration ahead of the US midterm elections.The White House said US officials were engaged in positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war. It also said the United States was facilitating significant oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz.There was no immediate public response from Gulf Arab governments to Iran's latest proposal. However, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Saudi Arabia was skeptical of the latest diplomatic push.Proposal resembles failed June agreementThe latest Iranian proposal resembles an interim agreement reached in June, but with a much shorter timetable.The earlier arrangement envisaged a 60-day interim period but subsequently collapsed after Iran resumed attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the supplied report.US President Donald Trump has said he is in no rush to reach a deal, even as elevated oil prices contribute to inflation.On the Iranian side, the proposal could face resistance from hard-liners who have criticised President Masoud Pezeshkian and Araghchi's diplomatic efforts.“If Trump calculates this arrangement is worthwhile and can bring political benefit before the midterms and reduce gas prices, perhaps we'll see flexibility not seen in previous weeks,” said Trita Parsi, executive vice president at the Quincy Institute think tank.Parsi also pointed to “deep suspicion” over whether Iran could use an agreement to buy time, move more oil and ease economic pressure.Qatar pushes diplomatic contactsIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian hosted Qatar's prime minister on Friday, in another sign of renewed diplomatic activity.Qatar has been involved in mediation between Tehran and Washington, including indirect contacts during the UN General Assembly.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that “if there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will.”But repeated failures to reach a lasting agreement have left both sides deeply distrustful. The United States and Israel have attacked Iran while it was engaged in nuclear talks, while Washington and Tehran have accused each other of violating the June agreement.Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran likely expected the proposal to face rejection.“The Iranians already know that the chances of this not being accepted by Trump are much higher than the opposite,” he wrote on X.“They want to show that they were ready for diplomacy and that it was the United States that, for the third time, decided to attack in the middle of a diplomatic track — something that people within (Iran’s) strategic community have been anticipating over the past few days,” he said.Yemen conflict complicates Hormuz proposalIran's proposal includes Lebanon, where Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah have largely observed a ceasefire. It remains unclear whether the plan would also cover the renewed conflict involving Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia.The Houthi attacks have added pressure to global markets and raised concerns about another strategic maritime chokepoint, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.Iran appears to view the Houthis' ability to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb as another source of leverage in negotiations with Washington.Araghchi also met his Saudi counterpart on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as Iranian officials held talks with representatives of countries involved in the wider regional conflict.Saudi Arabia has previously supported a return to negotiations and, according to the person familiar with the matter, had been open to an arrangement giving Iran a temporary role in managing the Strait of Hormuz.However, Saudi calculations changed after the Houthis seized Yemen's strategic Red Sea coast from pro-government forces and a vital Saudi pipeline came under attack.An earlier planned meeting of Gulf leaders in Oman to discuss an emerging Oman-Iran agreement on Hormuz was also cancelled after Saudi Arabia sought amendments to the proposed arrangement.Iran faces internal debate over diplomacyIranian leaders have sought to project unity, but the latest diplomatic moves have exposed divisions over how Tehran should respond to the United States.Some hard-liners have called for continued or intensified military action to secure greater concessions from Washington and have criticised Pezeshkian and Araghchi for pursuing negotiations.Firebrand lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei wrote on X that meeting with “the aggressor enemy” demonstrated weakness. articles.title: 'Surpreendente', diz professor que descobriu 1º felino em 100 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: 'Leopardus tilcayo' foi identificado nas florestas montanhosas bolivianas. Estudo também catalogou subespécie inédita no Peru.
articles.summary: 'Leopardus tilcayo' foi identificado nas florestas montanhosas bolivianas. Estudo também catalogou subespécie inédita no Peru.
articles.body:
A primeira descoberta de uma nova espécie de felino em mais de 100 anos só aconteceu devido a uma pesquisa liderada pelo professor gaúcho Eduardo Eizirik . Uma semana após a publicação na revista científica Current Biology, o estudo segue repercutindo pelo mundo.

🐯 A nova espécie de felino selvagem vive nas florestas montanhosas da Bolívia . O animal foi batizado de Leopardus tilcayo . No mesmo estudo, os pesquisadores identificaram ainda uma nova subespécie de felino que vive nas Yungas do Peru, denominada Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo.

"Eu esperava uma certa repercussão nos meios científicos e também com relação ao público geral, devido à natureza e raridade da descoberta. Mas não esperava que fosse tanta assim", comenta o pesquisador.

Docente da Escola de Ciências da Saúde e da Vida da Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS), em Porto Alegre , Eizirik conta que todo o processo: dos primeiros dados à publicação , levou aproximadamente 3 anos e envolveu pesquisadores de diferentes países.

"Vimos o quanto elas eram diferentes das outras, em um nível que indicava se tratar de uma espécie. Foi algo muito surpreendente."

Seu aluno de doutorado, Jonas Lescroart , coautor do artigo, já estava com análises bem avançadas dos genomas de felinos de várias regiões da América do Sul . Em paralelo, Eizirik e Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, da Bolívia, pesquisavam o tema. Eles então se juntaram e começaram a analisar amostras.

O professor destaca a importância da valorização da ciência para que mais descobertas aconteçam, o que, segundo ele, é essencial para a preservação da biodiversidade.

"Existem milhares de espécies desconhecidas no mundo, de todos os grandes grupos de animais, plantas, fungos e microrganismos, que exercem papéis muito importantes nos seus ecossistemas. E grande parte delas está ameaçada de extinção devido aos impactos humanos", explica.

Ele espera que seu projeto possa contribuir: "Uma repercussão internacional como essa, de um projeto liderado por uma equipe brasileira, pode ajudar a dar visibilidade à ciência brasileira de forma geral e estimular atores públicos e privados a investir mais na ciência", destaca.

Eizirik é graduado em Ciências Biológicas, com mestrado em Genética e Biologia Molecular pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) e doutorado em Biologia pela Universidade de Maryland em College Park (EUA) e pós-doutorado (2003) em Genética Evolutiva no Laboratório de Diversidade Genômica, Instituto Nacional de Câncer, Institutos Nacionais de Saúde (EUA).

'Tigrinho' boliviano: quem é o professor brasileiro que fez a primeira descoberta de felino em mais de 100 anos — Foto: Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz e Giordano Toldo/PUCRS

O Leopardus tilcayo foi descoberto após um filhote ser encontrado por um morador local em 2016 , na região de Nor Yungas, na Bolívia, e levado para o refúgio de animais La Senda Verde. A análise genética revelou que ele não pertencia à espécie que se imaginava, a Leopardus tigrinus . e sim a uma linhagem evolutivamente distinta e até então desconhecida .

Eizirik explica que esses gatos-do-mato podem ser considerados o que a ciência chama de espécie críptica.

A descoberta também apresenta uma mudança importante na compreensão da diversidade de um grupo de gatos-do-mato.

"São animais que apresentam aparência muito semelhante, mas são geneticamente diferentes e seguem histórias evolutivas independentes há centenas de milhares ou até milhões de anos. Essa semelhança visual fez com que diferentes espécies fossem, durante muito tempo, confundidas e classificadas como uma só", afirma o professor.

articles.title: Caso Master é foco dos candidatos ao Senado do RS em debate da RBS TV | G1
articles.standfirst: O debate foi realizado nos estúdios da RBS TV e mediado pelo jornalista Elói Zorzetto, na noite desta sexta-feira (25), em Porto Alegre.
articles.summary: O debate foi realizado nos estúdios da RBS TV e mediado pelo jornalista Elói Zorzetto, na noite desta sexta-feira (25), em Porto Alegre.
articles.body:
Em debate promovido pela RBS TV, os candidatos ao Senado pelo Rio Grande do Sul trocaram acusações sobre casos de corrupção no país, principalmente envolvendo o escândalo do Banco Master e as relações do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro com políticos e ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).

O debate foi realizado nos estúdios da RBS TV e mediado pelo jornalista Elói Zorzetto, na noite desta sexta-feira (25), em Porto Alegre . Participaram os candidatos Frederico Antunes (PSD), Rigotto (MDB), Manuela d'Ávila (PSOL), Marcel Van Hattem (Novo), Milton Cardoso (PSDB), Pimenta (PT), Renato Jaguarão (Cidadania), Sanderson (PL).

Ao longo de todos os blocos, os temas foram diversos. Segurança pública, economia, endividamento das famílias, bets, gastos públicos, feminicídios, crimes digitais, fundo constitucional, desenvolvimento econômico, mudanças climáticas e saúde estiveram no horizonte dos debates entre os concorrentes.

Dentro os temas, corrupção foi o que se sobressaiu. Os candidatos buscaram ligar o escândalo do Master ao espectro político dos seus adversários, citando mensagens e encontros de Vorcaro que têm vindo à tona.

Também falaram sobre a Suprema Corte, que está no centro dessa crise. Houve propostas para mudanças na forma de escolha dos ministros e pedido de abertura do processo de impeachment contra eles no Senado.

Candidatos ainda falaram sobre o fim das bets, proposto pelo presidente Lula (PT) em Medida Provisória (MP) assinada na tarde desta sexta-feira (25), que determina a proibição total de apostas de quota fixa no país .

No primeiro e no terceiro , os candidatos fizeram perguntas entre si com tema livre. Cada participante pôde escolher diretamente para quem fará a pergunta.

O tempo para a pergunta era de 30 segundos, enquanto as respostas tiveram duração de 1 minuto e 30 segundos. Na sequência, réplica e tréplica, ambas com 45 segundos.

Em cada um desses blocos, cada candidato fez uma pergunta e respondeu apenas uma vez.

O segundo bloco foi destinado a perguntas sobre temas definidos por sorteio. Após a definição do assunto, o candidato teve 30 segundos para formular a pergunta a um adversário escolhido por ele.

No primeiro bloco, os candidatos evitaram enfrentamentos. Prevaleceram as "dobradinhas", com concorrentes da mesma chapa debatendo entre si.

Foi o caso de Germano Rigotto (MDB) e Frederico Antunes (PSD), candidatos ao Senado da chapa de Gabriel Souza (MDB), que abriram o debate. A tônica se repetiu com Marcel van Hattem (Novo) e Ubiratan Sanderson (PL), que defendem a chapa de Luciano Zucco (PL), e com Paulo Pimenta (PT) e Manuela d’Ávila (PSOL), que representam a candidatura de Juliana Brizola (PDT).

Os candidatos falaram sobre a função de um senador da República e a postura que se deve ter no Congresso Nacional.

Renato Jaguarão (Cidadania) x Marcel van Hattem (Novo)

Os candidatos falaram sobre privilégios e sobre o fim da aposentadoria vitalícia para os governadores do Rio Grande do Sul, aprovado pela Assembleia Legislativa em 2021 .

Os candidatos falaram sobre segurança público e propostas para o fim das chamadas “saidinhas” para apenados no país.

Sandero (PL) x Renato Jaguarão (Cidadania)

Os candidatos falaram sobre feminicídio e proposta para tornar em crime o ódio contra as mulheres, tal qual ocorre com o racismo.

Os candidatos falaram sobre obras em estradas do Rio Grande do Sul.

Os candidatos falaram sobre o atual cenário no Congresso Nacional, sobre abertura de Comissão Parlamentar de Inquérito (CPI) para investigar o caso Master e pedidos de impeachment contra os ministros do STF.

Manuela d’Ávila (PSOL) x Milton Cardoso (PSDB)

Os candidatos falaram sobre escândalos de corrupção, entre eles o caso Master, e sobre proposta de novas leis para o combate à lavagem de dinheiro.

No bloco temático, os candidatos abordaram temas como segurança, desenvolvimento econômico, infraestrutura, reconstrução pós-enchente, agronegócio, previdência social, saúde, dívida pública.

"Muito obrigado, RBS TV, pela oportunidade. Nós estamos num momento muito difícil pelo qual passa o Brasil e passa o Rio Grande do Sul. Por isso, temos toda convicção. O Rio Grande merece mais, o Brasil merece mais. Formamos um time nacional de candidatos ao Senado. Aqui no Rio Grande do Sul, na nossa coligação, é Sanderson 222 e Marcelo van Hattem 300. Lá em Brasília, Flávio Bolsonaro, e aqui, no Piratini, Zucco governador. Vem conosco, pode confiar."

"Meu amigos e minhas amigas, eu estou muito feliz com o apoio que eu tenho recebido em todo o estado do Rio Grande do Sul. Eu peço o teu voto, peço que você me ajude nessa reta final a multiplicar e ampliar ainda mais a nossa campanha, para que a gente possa ter uma grande vitória no dia 4 de outubro. Eu conheço o Rio Grande do Sul, eu conheço o Brasília, eu tenho capacidade de diálogo, eu não faço diálogo com ódio, eu tenho amor por esse Rio Grande e eu conto contigo. Meu número é 131, É Pimenta senador, é a força do povo gaúcho."

"Gaúcho, chegou a oportunidade. Eu não quero reeleição. Eu estou entrando para ajudar com a experiência que eu tenho. Você pode transformar o Rio Grande do Sul. O Rio Grande precisa voltar a ser grande, elegendo pela primeira vez na história um senador da República sem um centavo de dinheiro público. Vem comigo, meu número é 455."

"Quero dizer que é um orgulho para mim poder caminhar junto com Gabriel Souza e Ernani Polo, nossos candidatos ao governo do Estado, número 15, caminhar junto com o Germano Rigotto, nosso candidato ao Senado da República, junto com o Frederico Antunes. E, obviamente, conversando com vocês, neste momento, pedir que, se já tem o primeiro voto, eu quero ser o teu segundo voto. E o meu número é 555. Conto com o teu apoio."

"Muito obrigado pela companhia, pela audiência e principalmente pelo teu voto: no Marcel van Hattem 300. Já são milhares de apoiadores estado afora e eu estou muito contente com essa caminhada. Uma caminhada que demonstra que a gente precisa ter proposta e precisa também ter sangue na veia para defender o que precisa ser feito lá em Brasília. Chega dessa situação que nós estamos vendo hoje no nosso país. Vamos defender o Rio Grande e mudar o Brasil. Peço teu voto, Marcel van Hattem 300, Sanderson 222. Governador, Zucco 22."

"Eu quero agradecer a oportunidade que a RBS nos dá, lembrar ao telespectador que a última pesquisa, a pesquisa saiu agora, da Quest da RBS, dá cinco candidatos embolados, cinco com empate técnico. Eu quero dizer que tem 30% que não definiram o seu voto. Eu espero contar com o voto de cada um que está nos assistindo e que pode confiar na minha história, no meu trabalho, na minha experiência. Eu vou honrar este voto. Frederico está comigo, junto com o Gabriel e com Ernani Polo."

"A hora é agora. O Brasil precisa de ti. Eu agradeço a tua audiência, mas eu quero te fazer um pedido. A partir de amanhã, vamos às ruas, às redes, garantir a nossa eleição. Garantir a eleição de Lula, de Juliana Brizola, minha e de Paulo Pimenta. Vai até as minhas redes, encontra um lugar onde buscar o material. Conversa com as tuas amigas, com os teus amigos. Nós temos a oportunidade de levar uma de nós para o Senado, por todas nós. Eu sou Manuela, 500."

"Agora, quem decide eleição não é pesquisa, não é poder, não é dinheiro. Quem decide eleição é tu, na urna. Tu é que vai dizer quem vai ser o teu senador. Se tu já tem o teu primeiro voto, dá o segundo voto para o Renato Jaguarão 234. Eu quero ser a tua voz no Senado. E é para ti, que, nesse momento, eu tiro o meu chapéu."

articles.title: Aeroporto de Macaé bate recorde histórico com 132 voos em um único dia | G1
articles.standfirst: Terminal registra maior movimentação diária desde 2020 impulsionado pelo setor offshore; aviação comercial com Guarulhos retorna em 2027.
articles.summary: Terminal registra maior movimentação diária desde 2020 impulsionado pelo setor offshore; aviação comercial com Guarulhos retorna em 2027.
articles.body:
Pista e estrutura ampliada garantem capacidade para absorver o aumento da demanda no município — Foto: Arquivo Secom

O Aeroporto de Macaé alcançou a maior movimentação diária da sua história recente, com o registro de 132 voos e o transporte de 1.275 passageiros em apenas 24 horas. O marco confirma uma trajetória constante de crescimento da atividade na região, impulsionada pela expansão do setor de energia e negócios no município.

O desempenho reflete os investimentos recentes na infraestrutura do terminal, que se consolidou como o único do país a operar o mercado offshore com duas pistas simultâneas. A ampliação do complexo aéreo já conta com obras em andamento de dois novos hangares, preparados para aumentar a eficiência no atendimento aos trabalhadores do setor e garantir o suporte necessário para novas altas no fluxo de passageiros.

Além do fortalecimento das operações voltadas ao segmento de óleo e gás, o terminal se prepara para dar um salto na aviação comercial regular. Está confirmada para fevereiro de 2027 a estreia de voos diretos operados pela LATAM ligando Macaé ao Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos, em São Paulo.

A nova rota commercial comercial garantirá três frequências semanais de ida e volta, conectando a cidade ao maior centro de conexões aéreas do Brasil. A novidade vai encurtar distâncias para empresários, moradores e turistas, integrando o município aos principais mercados nacionais e internacionais de forma direta.
